extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, students of poetics, and literary scholars interested in Aristotle's theory of poetry and dramatic craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging epic and tragic poetry (plot, character, diction, plausibility, and theatrical presentation) based on Aristotle's Poetics and scholarly commentary. Emphasises unity, probability, diction, and when «irrational» elements may be permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial self‑presentation (the poet speaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet in his own person should speak as little as possible; this is not what makes him an imitator. Homer, after a few prefatory words, at once brings in a man or woman or other personage, each with characteristic qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimise direct authorial intrusion into the work; introduce characters quickly and let their speech and action display character. Example: Homer’s few prefatory words then immediate character entrance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admittance and scope of the wonderful/irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the wonderful is admitted in Tragedy. The irrational, on which the wonderful depends for its chief effects, has wider scope in Epic poetry because the person acting is not seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow some irrational/wonderful elements, especially in epic (where action is narrated), but handle them so they please rather than jar; be sensitive to medium (stage vs narration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience inference fallacy exploited for fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The secret of Homeric fiction: people infer that if a later event is true the earlier presumed cause must also be true — a false inference the poet can exploit. Hence where the first thing is untrue it is unnecessary, if the second is true, to state the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use implied facts/causes rather than explicit falsehoods; rely on natural audience inferences to make a fiction convincing (example: the Odyssey Bath Scene).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities. The tragic plot must not consist of incidents which the reason rejects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including extraordinary events, choose versions that seem probable within the work’s internal logic or by received opinion rather than unlikely but technically possible details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and exclusion of irrational incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational incidents should, if possible, be excluded; or at least they should be outside the action of the play. Such incidents, however, once the plot is framed and an air of likelihood imparted, may be tolerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an irrational element is essential, keep it off-stage or narrated rather than enacted; if included in action, ensure the poet’s craft veils the absurdity (superior poets can make it acceptable; inferior poets make it intolerable). Examples: Oedipus’s ignorance of Laius’ death (off-stage), Electra’s messenger account, the silent Mysian who comes from Tegea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: elaboration only in pauses; avoid over-brilliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought. On the other hand, character and thought are merely obscured by a diction that is over brilliant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate language for moments without character-action content; avoid flashy diction that masks or diminishes characterization or the expression of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three objects a poet may imitate
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet, being an imitator, must of necessity imitate one of three objects — things as they were or are, things as they are said or thought to be, or things as they ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit (implicitly or explicitly) about which mode is used: realistic depiction, representation of belief/custom, or idealized norm; this affects plausibility and defenses against criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of poetic faults (essential vs accidental)
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the art of poetry there are two kinds of faults — those which touch its essence (inherent) and those which are accidental. If a poet imitates incorrectly through lack of capacity the error is essential; technical inaccuracies (e.g., medicine, horses) are accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between failures of imaginative capacity (serious) and correctable technical errors (less serious). Critics should consider which kind an error is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors against the rules: only justified if they attain the art’s end
rubrics_metrics.description: If the poet has represented things impossible according to the laws of his own art, it is an error; but the error may be justified if the end of the art is thereby attained. If the end could be as well attained without violating artistic rules, the error is not justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not violate technical/artistic constraints unless doing so produces a superior aesthetic or emotional effect that cannot otherwise be achieved; avoid gratuitous violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive stances for representation (as ought to be / as are / as said)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections that a description is untrue may be met by replying: 'the objects are as they ought to be' (Sophocles), or 'as they are' (Euripides), or 'this is what is commonly said' (tales about gods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticized for improbability/falsehood, ground the representation in one of these stances to justify its inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual judgement of action and speech
rubrics_metrics.description: In examining whether what has been said or done is right or wrong, we must not look merely to the particular speech or action, and ask whether it is in itself good or bad. We must also consider by whom it is said, to whom, when, in whose interest, or for what end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate lines and actions within their dramatic context (speaker, audience within the play, timing, and purpose). A morally dubious speech may be justified by motive or higher end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve apparent inconsistencies via dictional/grammatical means
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections may be resolved by due regard to diction: rare words, metaphor, change of accent, punctuation, ambiguity of construction, or usage may alter meaning and remove the objection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before condemning a passage as erroneous, analyse linguistic possibilities (alternate senses, metaphorical usage, accents, punctuation) and historical usage (e.g., words with different dialectal senses). Examples: οὐρῆας (mules vs sentinels), metaphorical 'all' = 'many', accent/punctuation changes in Hippias/Empedocles, ambiguity in πλέω.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polysemy: consider multiple senses of a word
rubrics_metrics.description: When a word seems to involve some inconsistency of meaning, we should consider how many senses it may bear in the particular passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine all plausible senses and select the reading that best fits context and avoids inconsistency; do not assume single literal meaning when multiple semantic senses are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hasty critical inferences (critic’s fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics jump at certain groundless conclusions; they pass adverse judgment and then proceed to reason on it, assuming the poet has said whatever they happen to think.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should test alternate interpretations and avoid reasoning from preconceived assumptions about what the poet 'must have meant.' Consider plausible readings and poet’s own tacit assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring impossibilities under poetic truth / received opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The impossible must be brought under the law of poetic truth, or of the higher reality, or of received opinion. A probable impossibility is to be preferred to a thing improbable and yet possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make extraordinary elements intelligible by appeal to poetic convention, elevated pattern (higher reality), or popular belief; this increases acceptance of the impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistency testing via dialectical refutation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inconsistencies should be examined by the same rules in dialectical refutation—whether the same thing is meant in the same relation and sense; whether the poet contradicts either what he says himself or what a sensible person would assume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for self-contradiction, equivocation, or incompatible assumptions; determine whether inconsistencies are real or resolvable by reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure of irrationality and moral depravity only when unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the irrational, and similarly depravity of character, are justly censured when there is no inner necessity for introducing them (e.g., Aegeus in Euripides, Menelaus in Orestes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include immoral or irrational character traits only when they are necessary for plot, theme, or a larger artistic end; otherwise they are properly criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five sources of critical objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Things are censured either as impossible, or irrational, or morally hurtful, or inconsistent, or inaccurate in respect of some special art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When answering criticism, identify which of these five charges is being made and apply the appropriate class of solutions (the text notes twelve heads of solution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish essential poetic errors from technical/art inaccuracies
rubrics_metrics.description: First consider whether the poet has represented things impossible according to the laws of his own art (an error); then whether the error touches the essentials of poetry or some accident of it (technical inaccuracy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise remediation of errors that undermine poetic essence; technical inaccuracies are less damning but should be corrected when they do not serve an essential end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestural/histrionic excess is a performance not poetic fault
rubrics_metrics.description: The censure of extravagant gesture or acting attaches not to the poetic but to the histrionic art; gesticulation may be equally overdone in epic recitation or lyrical competition as on the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a play, separate textual/poetic qualities from performance choices (gestures, dance). Excessive physicality is a performance problem, not necessarily a textual one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action and movement: not all action is condemnable
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all action is to be condemned—any more than all dancing—but only that of bad performers. Tragedy can produce its effect even without action; the fault is in bad execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use action and movement judiciously; ensure performers’ restraint and suitability to role, rather than avoiding action categorically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy’s superiority through concentration and accessory arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has all the epic elements and may use epic metre, with music and scenic effects as important accessories; the concentrated effect (shorter duration) is more pleasurable than one spread over long time (epic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For works aiming at intense, concentrated emotional effect, favour tragic form with careful integration of music and spectacle; unity and concentration are aesthetic virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and scale: multiple parts vs single action
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poems may contain many parts each with their own magnitude yet be perfect and an imitation of a single action. If a story is composed of several actions, if told concisely it may appear truncated; if told on proper epic scale it may seem weak in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match scope and scale to genre: long, multi‑part narratives suit epic; tragedy requires unity of action and concentrated scale; avoid truncation or undue dilution when changing form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of diction allowed in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The vehicle of expression is language—either common words or rare words or metaphors. There are also many modifications of language which we concede to the poets; the standard of correctness differs in poetry and politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets may legitimately use varied diction (rare words, metaphors, dialectal senses) but must do so with attention to clarity, context, and appropriateness to genre and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to treat representational 'errors' leniently
rubrics_metrics.description: If the end of the art is thereby attained — that is, if the effect of this or any other part of the poem is rendered more striking — an error may be justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh representational improprieties by their contribution to the poem’s artistic end; if they materially improve the poetic effect and are unavoidable, leniency is warranted.
